{{short description|American chemist}}
{{Infobox person/Wikidata | fetchwikidata=ALL | onlysourced=yes | dateformat = mdy|list=hlist}}

'''Margaret Ellen Mayo Tolbert''' (born November 24, 1943)<ref name="Kessler"/> is a [[chemistry|biochemist]] who worked as a professor and director of the Carver Research Foundation at [[Tuskegee University]], and was an administrative chemist at [[BP|British Petroleum]].<ref name="OH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= Margaret E.M. Tolbert |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/tolbert-margaret-e-m|website= [[Science History Institute]] |accessdate= 26 March 2018}}</ref><ref name="OralHistory">{{cite book|first=Jeannette E.  |last=Brown|title=Margaret E.M. Tolbert, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by Jeannette E. Brown at National Science Foundation Arlington, Virginia on 13 August 2009|date=13 August 2009 
|url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/tolbert_mem_0648_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Science History Institute|Chemical Heritage Foundation]] |accessdate= 26 March 2018 }}</ref>
From 1996 to 2002 she served as director of the [[New Brunswick Laboratory]], becoming the first African American and the first woman in charge of a [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy]] lab.<ref name="Managerial">{{cite web|title=Managerial Leadership in Government|url=http://www.blackengineer.com/events/winners%20bios/margaret%20tolbert.shtml|publisher=BlackEngineer.com|accessdate=13 May 2014}}</ref><ref name="Spangenburg">{{cite book|last1=Spangenburg|first1=Ray|last2=Moser|first2=Kit|title=African Americans in Science, Math, and Invention|date=2003|publisher=Facts On File|location=New York, NY|isbn=978-1-4381-0774-5|pages=211–212|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XSOZ8kF5ynEC&q=Margaret%20E.%20M.%20Tolbert&pg=PA211|chapter=Tolbert, Margaret Ellen Mayo}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Margaret Ellen Mayo was born in [[Suffolk, Virginia]], to Jessie Clifford "Clifton" and Martha Taylor Artis Mayo.<ref name="Spangenburg"/> Her mother died when she was quite young,<!-- I've seen both 3 and 7 given as her age --> and her father  a few years later.  She and her siblings were raised for several years by her grandmother Fannie Mae Johnson Mayo,<ref name="Kessler"/> and after her grandmother  became ill, by the older sister, Audrey Mae.<ref name="Marable">{{cite news|last1=Marable|first1=Christina|title='Resilience in the Face of Adversity': The Life of Dr. Margaret E. M. Tolbert|url=http://www.maceandcrown.com/2016/07/26/resilience-face-adversity-life-dr-margaret-e-m-tolbert/|accessdate=12 December 2016|work=Mace & Crown|date=July 26, 2016}}</ref> Margaret and her five siblings were kept together in spite of financial difficulties.<ref name="Kessler">{{cite book|last1=Kessler|first1=James H.|first2= J.S.|last2= Kidd|first3=Renee A.|last3= Kidd|first4= Katherine A.|last4= Morin|title=Distinguished African American scientists of the 20th century|date=1996|publisher=Oryx Press|location=Phoenix, Ariz.|isbn=0897749553|pages=[https://archive.org/details/distinguishedafr00kess/page/317 317]–320|url=https://archive.org/details/distinguishedafr00kess|url-access=registration|accessdate=12 December 2016}}</ref> The city was strongly segregated, with different areas at the beach and different entrances and drinking fountains in stores and movie theaters.<ref name="Marable"/>

Margaret Mayo attended Ida V. Easter Graded School, and then East Suffolk Junior High. She walked two miles to reach junior high school and was still the top in her class.<ref name="Kessler" /> Her hard work continued through high school. She worked as a maid to help her family while she took advanced placement classes.<ref name="Kessler" /> A well-off African-American couple for whom she worked, Mrs. and Mrs. S. A. Cook, were supportive, sponsoring her as a [[debutante]] and encouraging her to attend university.<ref name="chemheritage">{{Cite web|url=http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/online-resources/chemistry-in-history/themes/chemical-education-and-public-policy/public-policy/tolbert.aspx|title=Margaret E. M. Tolbert|website=Chemical Heritage Foundation |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160712164930/http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/online-resources/chemistry-in-history/themes/chemical-education-and-public-policy/public-policy/tolbert.aspx|archivedate=July 12, 2016}}</ref> She graduated from East Suffolk High School in 1963 at the top of her class of 99 students, and was its [[valedictorian]].<ref name="Resilience"/>

==University education==
Margaret enrolled in the [[Tuskegee Institute]], an action enabled primarily by the availability of financial aid. The Cooks drove her to Alabama, and introduced her to friends at Tuskegee, the Howells.<ref name="chemheritage"/><ref name="Resilience"/>{{rp|96–97}} At the time Tuskegee was actively involved in the civil rights movement.<ref name="Resilience">{{cite book|last1=Tolbert|first1=Margaret Ellen Mayo|title=Resilience in the Face of Adversity: A Suffolkian's Life Story|date=2015|publisher=Balboa Press|location=Bloomington, IN|isbn=9781504331982|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HUADCgAAQBAJ&pg=PT19|accessdate=12 December 2016}}</ref>{{rp|95–98}}   At Tuskegee University, Margaret enrolled in chemistry with a minor in mathematics.<ref name="OralHistory"/>{{rp|21}} Margaret was a student research assistant under the mentorship of C. J. Smith and L. F. Koons of the Tuskegee Institute Department of Chemistry. She also participated in summer research at [[North Carolina Central University|Central State College]] in [[Durham, North Carolina]], and at [[Argonne National Laboratory]] (ANL). As an assistant at Tuskegee, she studied the conductivity and [[electrical resistance]] of different chemicals in water solutions. At ANL, she studied the electrical resistance and chemical combinations of [[uranium]].<ref name="Kessler" /> She graduated from Tuskegee in 1967 with a B.S. degree.<ref name="Kessler" /><ref name="Spangenburg"/> She also married briefly and had a son.<ref name="OralHistory"/>{{rp|21–23}}

She earned her [[Master of Science]] degree in analytical chemistry from [[Wayne State University]] in 1968,<ref name="Kessler" /> and returned briefly to Tuskegee, where she supervised chemistry projects and taught mathematics (1969–1970).<ref name="Warren">{{cite book|last1=Warren|first1=Wini|title=Black women scientists in the United States|date=1999|publisher=Indiana University Press|location=Bloomington, Ind. [u.a.]|isbn=9780253336033|pages=[https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr/page/263 263]–264|url=https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr|url-access=registration}}</ref> She was then recruited to  [[Brown University]]  where she defended her thesis in 1973 and received her doctorate degree in biochemistry in 1974.<ref name="Kessler" /><ref name="OralHistory"/>{{rp|21–23,28}}  Her research involved [[signal transduction]] in rat liver cells. Her research advisor at Brown was John Nicholas Fain of the Division of Medical Sciences.<ref name="OralHistory"/>{{rp|25–27}} While at Brown she married her second husband, Henry Hudson Tolbert.<ref name="chemheritage"/>

The research conducted by Margaret while she was a student at Brown University was "... among the first studies in signal transduction to point out that there are rapid effects of ligands that did not involve RNA or protein synthesis and occur by some intracellular messenger other than cyclic AMP"<ref name="Resilience"/><!-- search displayed quote but not page number --> according to Fain.  She also taught science and mathematics at the Opportunities Industrialization Center in [[Providence, Rhode Island]], while completing her graduate studies.<ref name="Spangenburg"/>

==Further career==
After earning her doctorate degree, she returned to Tuskegee as a faculty member and researcher in the chemistry department, continuing her rat liver research (1973–1976).<ref name="Spangenburg"/><ref name="Warren"/>  She taught at [[Florida A&M University]] for two years (1977–1979) and was an associate dean there<ref name="Warren"/> before accepting a short-term visiting research position at  the International Institute of Cellular and Molecular Pathology (ICP) in [[Brussels, Belgium]] in 1979.<ref name="Kessler" /> This position was made possible by a grant from the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.<ref name="Spangenburg"/> She then accepted a short-term visiting research position at Brown University, again working on the biochemistry of the liver.<ref name="Kessler" />

In 1979,<ref name="Warren"/> Tolbert returned to Tuskegee as the first female director of The Carver Research Foundation of Tuskegee University<ref name="Spangenburg"/> and as provost of the university, holding these positions for eight years.<ref name="Kessler" /> She also continued to research the effects of drugs on the human liver.<ref name="Warren"/>

Other institutions at which she has conducted research include: [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]] (Biomedical Institute, Summer 1974), University of Texas Medical School at Houston (Department of Neurobiology and Anatomy; Department of Pharmacology; Summer 1977), and the NARACOM/ARIEM (Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine) in Natick, MA (between 1980 and 1985).

In 1987, Tolbert joined the research department of [[BP|British Petroleum]].<ref name="Kessler" /><ref name="Warren"/> She was involved as a corporate planner in the merger of BP and [[Standard Oil of Ohio]].<ref name="Kessler" /> Between 1990 and 1993, she was In 1994, she worked briefly as a consultant for the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]]<ref name="Warren"/> developing international research programs.<ref name="Kessler" />

Tolbert then accepted the position of division director at the [[Argonne National Laboratory]].  In 1996 she resigned to become director of the [[New Brunswick Laboratory]]. She was the first African American and the first woman in charge of a [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy]] lab.<ref name="OralHistory"/>{{rp|58–63}}<ref name="Spangenburg"/>  She was director of the New Brunswick Laboratory from 1996 to 2002.<ref name="Managerial"/> She served on Presidential Committees on Education and Technology.<ref name="Spangenburg"/> As director of the New Brunswick Laboratory, she was involved in projects to prevent the spread of nuclear materials and weapons technology, the preparation of nuclear reference materials for the standardization of instruments, assessment of worldwide measurement capabilities at nuclear laboratories, and measurement of nuclear material from worldwide samples.<ref name="chemheritage"/>

As of September 22, 2002, Tolbert became Senior Advisor to the Office of Integrative Activities (OIA), promoting activities at the [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF) that increase the participation of underrepresented groups (women, minorities, and people with disabilities) in science and engineering. She has acted as Executive Secretary and NSF Executive Liaison to the Committee on Equal Opportunity in Science and Engineering.<ref name="BlackIvy">{{cite web|title=Alumni Spotlight: Dr. Margaret Ellen Mayo Tolbert|url=http://www.theleagueonline.org/alumni_spotlight.php?submit=detail&uid=83|website=Black Ivy Alumni League|accessdate=12 December 2016}}</ref> She retired from the NSF in December 2011.<ref name="Banks"/><ref name="NSF2012">{{cite web|title=Committee on Equal Opportunities in Science and Engineering Meeting Minutes February 28, 2012 |date=February 28, 2012|url=https://www.nsf.gov/od/oia/activities/ceose/minutes/CEOSE_MeetingMinutes_Feb2012.pdf|website=National Science Foundation|page=4|accessdate=12 December 2016}}</ref>

==Honors==
Tolbert has received a number of awards and honors.<ref name="BlackIvy"/>  In 1998, Tolbert was elected as a member of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS). She is also a member of the [[American Association of University Women]] (AAUW), the [[American Chemical Society]] (ACS), and the Organization of Black Scientists.<ref name="Spangenburg"/>

==Autobiography==
In 2015, she published an autobiography, ''Resilience in the Face of Adversity: A Suffolkian’s Life Story'' (Balboa Press, 2015).<ref name="Banks">{{cite news|last1=Banks|first1=Mary B.|title=Retired scientist recounts her journey in new memoir|url=http://baltimoretimes-online.com/news/2016/jul/01/retired-scientist-recounts-her-journey-new-memoir/|accessdate=12 December 2016|work=Baltimore Times|date=July 1, 2016}}</ref>
